{"id": "1:7/q17", "question": "What does divine anger mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the divine expression names an attribute, will to punish, condemnation, or the punishment itself.", "positions": [{"id": "1:7/q17/p1", "position": "Divine anger is the will to punish or avenge", "reasons": "THALABI reporting قوم: One group explains God's anger as His will to take vengeance on sinners. MAWARDI reporting unattributed: Another interpretation takes wrath as the will to exact vengeance, since the linguistic root implies harshness, which cannot be ascribed to God. MAWARDI-FULL: A second account interprets God's anger as a will to punish; anger linguistically means severity, a quality unsuitable for God. WAHIDI-QT: Those under wrath are Jews; God's wrath means His willing punishment. WAHIDI-WAJIZ: Those under divine anger are the Jews; God's anger means His willing punishment. BAGHAWI-FULL: Those under wrath are people whose path incurred God’s anger; divine anger is the will to punish sinners, but does not befall sinful believers, only disbelievers. KASHSHAF: God's anger is His will to avenge sinners and punish them, acting as a king does when angry with a subordinate. KASHSHAF-FULL: God's anger means His will to take vengeance on sinners, punish them, and treat them as a king does those under his authority. TABRISI: Divine anger is God's will to impose deserved punishment, curse the people, and disavow them; its root denotes severity. QURTUBI: Divine anger can mean God's will to punish, an essential attribute, or the punishment itself, an attribute of action; a hadith says charity extinguishes the Lord's anger. QURTUBI-FULL: Alayhim is grammatically understood as “wrath fell upon them”; wrath linguistically means severity, while in God’s attribute it is either His will to punish or punishment itself. NASAFI: God’s anger means His will to take vengeance on liars and punish them, treating them as a king does those under his authority when angry. NASAFI-FULL: The first “upon them” is an object and the second is a subject; God's anger means His will to exact revenge and impose punishment on deniers. ABUHAYYAN: God's anger may mean His intent to requite a sinner, making it an attribute of essence because His knowledge precedes creation and sin; alternatively it is imposing punishment, an attribute of action. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Divine anger can mean the will to punish, an attribute of essence given God’s prior knowledge, or the act of inflicting punishment, an attribute of action. SAMIN-DURR: Anger is described as the heart's blood surging in intent to take revenge; a prophetic report warns against anger and describes its bodily signs. SAMIN-DURR: Alternative definitions make anger a heart's change toward something disliked, or distinguish divine action-attribute when it means punishment from essential attribute when it means the will to punish. ALUSI reporting السعد: In his commentary on al-Miftāḥ, al-Saʿd defines anger as a movement of the soul whose origin is the will to take revenge. ALUSI reporting السعد: In his commentary on al-Kashshāf, al-Saʿd defines divine anger as the will to take revenge. ALUSI reporting الزمخشري: Al-Zamakhsharī explains God’s anger as His will to punish sinners, bringing punishment upon them as an angry king does to subjects under his authority. ALUSI-FULL: The source gives several technical definitions of anger: a movement arising from desire for vengeance, the will to exact vengeance, or an inward condition producing outward movement; a report likens anger to a glowing ember in the heart. ALUSI-FULL reporting الكشاف: Al-Zamakhshari explains God's anger as His will to exact vengeance and punish sinners, acting as an angry ruler acts toward a subordinate. ELMALILI: When attributed to God, anger means its ultimate end, the will to retaliate or impose punishment, and is compatible with merciful lordship: punishing an oppressor serves mercy to the oppressed."}, {"id": "1:7/q17/p2", "position": "Divine anger is punitive action or its effects", "reasons": "TAB: The wrathful are identified with those described in the Qur'an as cursed and punished for disobedience; God also shows the community the way to avoid their fate. | mentions 5:60 TAB reporting بعضهم: One view explains God's anger as His imposing punishment on those He is angry with, in this world or the next. | mentions 43:55, 5:60 TAB reporting ابن عباس: In Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation, the prayer asks God to inspire true monotheistic religion, spare the worshippers His anger like the Jews, and keep them from Christian error and punishment. TAB: Recounting punishments for disobedience warns people away from sin and from incurring God's anger, whose consequences lead to destruction. TAB-FULL: Those under anger are the people God describes as cursed and punished in Qur'an 5:60; He informs believers of their fate and shows them the route to salvation out of mercy. | mentions 5:60 TAB-FULL reporting بعضهم: One theological account says God's anger is the imposition of punishment in this life or the next, citing the drowning of Pharaoh's people and the punishment described in Qur'an 5:60. | mentions 43:55, 5:60 TAB-FULL reporting بعضهم: A third account treats anger as a real divine attribute, intelligible by affirmation but unlike human anger, which involves agitation, pain, or harm; it is an attribute like knowledge and power without creaturely limitations. TAB-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas glosses the astray as Christians whom God led astray through their fabrication about Him; the prayer asks for the true monotheistic faith, protection from Jewish wrath and Christian error, and mercy to prevent their punishment. THALABI reporting قيل: Another explanation calls anger a kind of punishment opposite to divine pleasure. MAWARDI reporting unattributed: A fourth interprets wrath as a kind of punishment named anger, just as God’s blessings are named mercy. MAWARDI-FULL: A fourth account calls a kind of punishment anger, just as God's bounty is called mercy. BAGHAWI: “Not those angered” means a path other than that of those God wills to punish for disobedience. IBNATIYYA: The author says scripture repeatedly describes God’s wrath against Jews, citing their incurring wrath and the punishment of Sabbath-breakers. | mentions 2:61, 3:112, 5:60, 2:65 IBNATIYYA: Here divine wrath means God’s manifesting ordeals, punishments, humiliation, and similar signs that He has emphatically distanced them from His mercy. IBNATIYYA-FULL: God's anger means that he exposes them to trials, punishments, and humiliation, showing their decisive removal from his mercy. RAZI-FULL: Razi poses the problem that divine anger follows knowledge of human sin: if God's knowledge is eternal, why create people destined for endless punishment and why create what He is angry with? RAZI-FULL: Human anger is a bodily change, impossible for God; psychological terms applied to God signify their final effect, so divine anger means willing harm, while divine modesty means leaving an act. QURTUBI: Arabic anger connotes severity: a harsh person is ghadub, a fierce serpent al-ghadub, and a folded camel-hide shield ghadba for its toughness. QURTUBI-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A hadith says charity extinguishes the Lord’s wrath, treating wrath as an attribute of action when it means the punishment. BAYDAWI-FULL: Divine anger denotes its ultimate effect, punishment; عليهم is a passive-subject phrase, unlike the earlier construction, and لا reinforces the negation in غير. ABUHAYYAN: The passive wording for those angered is tactful in a humble plea: the worshipper attributes favor to the One asked for guidance but avoids confronting Him with the description of vengeance. SAMIN-DURR: When attributed to God, anger means retribution; غضبت لفلان is said of a living person and غضبت به of a dead one. BURSEVI: Divine anger cannot mean its human beginning, so it denotes its end or effect, such as punishment, retribution, or painful seizure. BURSEVI: Divine anger perfects the function of the left hand: mercy and severity have distinct effects, and severity completes what cannot be repaired by mercy. | mentions 39:67 ELMALILI: A temporary punishment or pain that prepares future blessings does not make someone one of those under wrath; outcomes determine the judgment, as 2:155 illustrates. | mentions 2:155 IBNASHUR: Because literal anger entails change, which cannot apply to God, the attribution means its consequence—punishment, humiliation, or worldly exclusion—or a representational metaphor. IBNASHUR: Divine anger is God’s treatment of those who oppose guidance, ranging up to the lasting punishment of polytheists and hypocrites; dislike is lesser, and both differ from creative will. | mentions 39:7, 6:112, 10:99 IBNASHUR reporting بعض ملوك الفرس: An unnamed Persian king said his reign endured because he punished according to the offense rather than according to anger. IBNASHUR-FULL: Divine anger means God's treatment of those who leave guidance and disobey, culminating in punishment; anger, dislike, pleasure, and love differ from creative will. | mentions 39:7, 6:112, 10:99 IBNASHUR-FULL: God cannot literally undergo anger or change; the attribution must mean its effects, such as punishment, humiliation, curse, or exclusion, or function as a representational metaphor."}, {"id": "1:7/q17/p3", "position": "Divine anger is condemnation or blame", "reasons": "TAB reporting بعضهم: Another view takes divine anger as God's blame of people and their deeds, and verbal condemnation of them. TAB: Jews and Christians are both astray and under wrath; God labels each group by a real, recognizable trait, without implying that it lacks the other's blameworthy traits. TAB-FULL reporting بعضهم: A second account understands divine anger as blame for their conduct and verbal reproach or insult. TAB-FULL: Both Jews and Christians are astray and under wrath, but God labels each by a true, recognizable characteristic,

without listing every blameworthy trait of either group. THALABI reporting قيل: A third explanation defines anger as condemnation of sinners for the ugliness of their acts. MAWARDI reporting unattributed: A third interpretation is that God’s wrath means His condemnation of them. MAWARDI-FULL: A third account interprets God's anger as His condemnation of them. IBNKATHIR: Qurʾanic references to Jewish anger and wrongdoing support the identification: Israel's children incur anger for rejecting revelation and are condemned for sin and failure to stop wrongdoing. | mentions 2:90, 5:60, 5:78, 5:79 BIQAI-FULL reporting الحرالي: Al-Harali defines the condemned as those who intentionally oppose guidance and thereby incur divine wrath, or those who turn toward guidance then stray without intending to. | mentions 93:6 ITQAN: The verse explicitly attributes favor to God, but avoids saying “those with whom You were angry,” shifting expression so anger is not verbally attributed to God in direct address. IBNASHUR-FULL: Angered people represent deliberate religious disregard or far-fetched interpretation, while astray people err through poor understanding or inattention; both are blameworthy. IBNASHUR-FULL: Anger for oneself is blameworthy, but anger defending public and religious interests is praiseworthy; the Prophet did not get angry for himself but did for God's limits. SAMARRAI-ASRAR: The Fātiḥa explicitly attributes favor to God (‘You bestowed favor’) while describing the blameworthy as those under anger and those astray. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT: The passive المغضوب عليهم leaves the agent open so the condemned face anger from God, angels, people, and even their own skins. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT: Repeating لا ensures exclusion of either condemned group on its own; without it the wording might exclude only those who combine anger and error, as the two-part prohibition analogy shows. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT: The angered oppose the favored just as anger opposes grace; the chapter's ending gathers its opening praise, judgment, exclusive worship, reliance, and guidance into the fates of the condemned."}, {"id": "1:7/q17/p4", "position": "Anger is a real divine attribute unlike human agitation", "reasons": "TAB reporting بعضهم: A third view affirms an intelligible divine attribute called anger, while distinguishing it from human agitation and affirming that God's essence is free of affliction. TAB-FULL reporting السدي عن أبي مالك وأبي صالح عن ابن عباس ومرة الهمداني عن ابن مسعود وناس من أصحاب النبي: The report attributed through al-Suddī to these early authorities identifies those under wrath as Jews. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting عدي بن حاتم: A report from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, attributed to the Prophet, identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; no grading is stated. WAHIDI-BASIT: For the standard reading, the sense is the path of those favored who are neither under wrath nor astray; denying these traits implicitly attributes them to others, supporting implication in discourse. RAZI-FULL reporting أصحابنا: Razi's Ash'arite school reads the sequence as God's anger causing their misguidance; the reverse would make a human attribute affect God, which is impossible. BAYDAWI: When anger is attributed to God, it denotes the final outcome or endpoint, not an emotion in God. IBNKATHIR: The verse attributes favor directly to God, leaves the agent of anger unexpressed although God is its true agent, and assigns misguidance to those who embody it although He misleads by His decree; cited verses affirm His exclusive control of guidance and misguidance. | mentions 58:14, 18:17, 7:186 BURHAN reporting قيل: One explanation says praise uses third person because it ranks below worship, while direct address elevates the worshipper's encounter; similarly, blessing is explicitly attributed to God but anger is phrased obliquely as a matter of etiquette. | mentions 6:101 BURSEVI: A common reading identifies those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians, but neither group's label is exclusive because Scripture attributes both traits to both. ALUSI: Following the early generations, al-Ālūsī affirms anger as an eternal divine attribute fitting God’s majesty without specifying how or claiming to know its reality, like mercy. ALUSI: The blessing is directly attributed to God as a deferential appeal for guidance to those whose favor is established; anger is put in the passive and left unassigned out of courtesy in a humble request for kindness. ALUSI-FULL: Alusi follows the early community: anger is a divine attribute befitting God, whose reality and manner are unknown, like mercy; “My mercy precedes My anger” concerns the greater or earlier manifestation of mercy. ELMALILI: Qur'an also attributes divine wrath to disbelievers generally and describes those who reject God's way as far astray, supporting the comprehensive reading. | mentions 16:106"}, {"id": "1:7/q17/p5", "position": "Human anger is bodily or psychological agitation; the divine usage is interpreted accordingly", "reasons": "ALUSI: A definition in Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid describes anger as a state of the soul followed by the spirit’s outward motion seeking revenge; another account calls it a change when the heart’s blood boils. ALUSI: A hadith warns people to beware of anger, likening it to a glowing ember in the heart and pointing to swollen neck veins and reddened eyes; no grading or source is given here. IBNASHUR: Human anger is a psychic response to what displeases, producing aversion and harsh treatment; revenge may follow but is not essential, contrary to those who make it definitional. IBNASHUR-FULL: Human anger is a psychological aversion that can lead to harsh treatment and sometimes revenge; revenge is not essential to anger, whose intensity varies among people and customs. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT reporting التفسير القيم: Corrupt knowledge produces misguidance and corrupt intention produces anger; these are the two root diseases of the heart. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT: The knowing disobedience of Iblis was the first sin; after it, he vowed to mislead humanity, so anger appropriately precedes misguidance. | mentions 4:119"}, {"id": "1:7/q17/p6", "position": "In ghayr al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim wa-lā al-ḍāllīn, the first lā is an extra particle completing the phrase, effectively ‘and the straying.’", "reasons": "MAJAZ: In ghayr al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim wa-lā al-ḍāllīn, the first lā is an extra particle completing the phrase, effectively ‘and the straying.’"}, {"id": "1:7/q17/p7", "position": "Anger means being left to oneself, while error means losing God's protection and attachment.", "reasons": "SULAMI reporting بعضهم: Anger means being left to oneself, while error means losing God's protection and attachment."}, {"id": "1:7/q17/p8", "position": "Al-Zajjāj says lā may coordinate with ghayr because ghayr already carries negation, effectively meaning neither those angered nor those astray;
